documents: Li, R. (2022). Uranium enrichment associated with geothermal alteration: An example from Rehai, Tengchong volcanic area of China. Geological Journal 57(10), 4139–4151 (published paper, PDF)

entry.evidence: the relationship between uranium mineralization and the active geothermal system is rarely examined

steps.action: Takes from Zhu & Tong (1987) the alteration zoning at Rehai and the presence of pitchblende and coffinite in surface sinters at Tengchong.
steps.quote: uranium minerals such as pitchblende and coffinite were found present in surface sinters precipitated from hot springs at Tengchong

steps.action: Poses the question of how uranium mineralization relates to the active geothermal system, noting that the elemental geochemistry of the spring deposits has not been studied.
steps.quote: the relationship between uranium mineralization and the active geothermal system is rarely examined

steps.action: Collects published high U concentrations in tufas, travertines and sinters elsewhere (California, Jordan, worldwide sinters) as context.
steps.quote: high uranium concentrations have been reported in the Miocene tufas in California

steps.action: Designs a comparison of stable isotopes, trace elements and REE across hot spring water, spring deposits and altered sandstones at the Rehai geothermal field.
steps.quote: the Rehai geothermal field (RHGF) in the Tengchong volcanic area has been selected to compare the geochemical attributes

steps.action: Samples five waters (one borehole, three pools, one flow path) in May 2019, filters them, and measures trace elements by ICP-MS and δD/δ18O with a liquid water isotope analyser.
steps.quote: Concentrations of trace elements in the waters were measured using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry

steps.action: Checks isotope precision against replicate analyses of three laboratory standards.
steps.quote: Analytical precision was better than ±0.6‰ for δD and ± 0.2‰ for δ18O based on replicate analyses of three standards

steps.action: Uses REE concentrations of Rehai hot spring waters taken from Xiao et al. (2010) and Hou et al. (2013) instead of measuring them.
steps.quote: The rare earth element (REE) concentrations for the hot spring waters from Rehai (see Table S1) were modified from Xiao

steps.action: Collects five hot spring deposits and analyses them by XRD (semi-quantitative mineralogy), thin sections, SEM-EDS, and ICP-MS after HNO3–HF digestion for trace elements and REE+Y.
steps.quote: Five hot spring deposits were collected

steps.action: Applies oxide interference corrections using a tuning solution before ICP-MS calibration and reports typical accuracy.
steps.quote: Accuracy is typically within 10 relative percent.

steps.action: Takes the trace element, REE and U concentrations of the altered Neogene host sandstones from Xiao et al. (2017).
steps.quote: The trace element and REE concentrations of altered host rocks (i.e., Neogene sandstones) in Rehai came from Xiao et al. (2017)

steps.action: Plots water δD–δ18O against the global and local meteoric water lines (Figure 3) and reports U and other trace contents of the waters.
steps.quote: Almost all the plots of D-O isotopes of hot spring waters distribute along the global meteoric water line

steps.action: Describes field morphology, mineralogy (sinters of amorphous silica; alunogen, tamarugite, gypsum, anhydrite sulfates), microfabrics, U (max 27 ppm in tamarugite) and REE+Y patterns of the deposits.
steps.quote: The domal samples (Figure 2a) formed of amorphous silica minerals belong to sinters.

steps.action: Compares crust-normalized trace element patterns: deposits are enriched relative to waters, and the altered sandstones have higher Pb, Th and U than the deposits.
steps.quote: the hot spring deposits from RHGF are relatively enriched in Zn

steps.action: Retains meteoric water as the main source of the geothermal water, based on the isotope relation and similarity to local precipitation.
steps.quote: suggests that meteoric water acts as the main water source of the geothermal waters

steps.action: Names enhanced water–rock interaction and/or evaporation as explanations of the positive δ18O shift, taken from published work and not discriminated.
steps.quote: may be related to enhanced water-rock interactions (Du et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2016) and/or evaporation due to varying temperatures

steps.action: Attributes the REE+Y in the water to water–rock interaction, and the high REE at Zhenzhu Spring to acidity, citing low-pH REE mobility.
steps.quote: could only be derived from the surrounding host rocks through water-rock interactions

steps.action: Interprets the negative Eu anomalies of the deposits as precipitation from spring water under reduced conditions, consistent with shared REE patterns and with negative Eh values from Zhang et al. (2008).
steps.quote: the distinctly negative Eu anomalies (Figure 5a) indicate their precipitation from hot spring water under reduced conditions

steps.action: Derives from U(VI) mobility and the cited Eh values the expectation that Zhenzhu Spring water should carry more U than Dagunguo.
steps.quote: the spring water at Zhenzhu Spring is supposed to contain a higher amount of U than that at Dagunguo

steps.action: Compares that expectation with the measured water U concentrations (Table 1) and finds them coherent.
steps.quote: This is coherent with the fact that the [...] concentrations of water at Zhenzhu Spring are the highest

steps.action: Compares HFSE and Cs enrichment and the REE+Y patterns of the altered sandstones with published flat terrigenous patterns and with the spring water patterns, and infers hydrothermal alteration.
steps.quote: are different from the terrigenous rocks which are characterized by a flat distribution pattern

steps.action: Proposes that the HREE enrichment of the sandstones comes from preferential HREE mobilization into clay minerals, citing illitization studies.
steps.quote: their HREE-enrichment pattern may be derived from the preferential mobilization of HREE into the clay minerals

steps.action: Orders U concentrations across reservoirs: meteoric water ≤ hot spring water < spring deposits < altered sandstones.
steps.quote: [...] concentrations measured in this study generally follow the order below.

steps.action: Proposes U leaching from granite reservoir rocks, transport up active faults, and precipitation on decompression (mechanism cited from Li 1992 and Li et al. 1997), illustrated in Figure 8.
steps.quote: U in the spring water may come from leaching of U-rich reservoir rocks (e.g., granite) by meteoric water and/or circulated geothermal water

steps.action: Compares the 27 ppm U of the tamarugite deposit with published sinters (Nevada, Tibet) and tufas.
steps.quote: The value is much higher than the U concentrations of sinters from northern Nevada

steps.action: Attributes the difference between deposit types to differential fractionation of uranyl carbonate and sulfate complexes and SiO2-colloid-adsorbed U.
steps.quote: It probably reflects the differential fractionation behaviour among uranyl carbonate complex, uranyl sulfate complex, and uranium adsorbed by SiO2 colloid.

steps.action: Compares the altered-sandstone U (14–36 ppm) with typical rock values (Kathren 1984) and attributes the excess to U adsorption on clay minerals.
steps.quote: higher than the typical sandstone, shale, limestone (1–10 ppm), and even granite (15 ppm)

steps.action: Keeps a multi-cycle leaching–transport–decompression–fixation model of U enrichment, citing similar cases in Jordan and South Australia, and proposes sulfates and clay alteration zones as uranium exploration targets.
steps.quote: uranium enrichment is probably a complex process involving multiple cycles of leaching, transportation, decompression, and fixation

tree.answer: U enrichment in hot spring deposits and altered sandstones of an active geothermal field
Concentrations measured directly; the enrichment mechanism is not observed
Explain the U enrichment mechanism by comparing water, deposits and host rocks
Rivals only for side questions (δ18O shift, solute origin); none for the U mechanism
One derived expectation (higher-Eh Zhenzhu water carries more U), checked against data
Conditions found in a live geothermal system, not set
Not tested beyond analytical precision and accuracy checks
Mechanism kept as 'probably' related to multi-cycle leaching, transport, decompression, fixation

end.claim: U enrichment in the Rehai spring deposits and altered sandstones probably results from multiple cycles of U leaching from granites, upward transport along faults by geothermal water, decompression, and fixation, so geothermal alteration zones are potential uranium exploration targets.

decisive_move.sentence: The new ICP-MS measurements of the hot spring deposits (Table 2), especially 27 ppm U in Zhenzhu tamarugite, set beside the cited sandstone and water data, make the U-concentration order on which the enrichment model rests.

gates.evidence: Sampling was a comparative survey of waters and deposits; no stated hypothesis directed it (p. 4140). The only check that could have failed is the Eh-based expectation that Zhenzhu water carries more U, compared with Table 1 (p. 4148). The multi-cycle U model itself is not tested (p. 4149). Nothing is reported as fixed in advance.

imports.item: Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (Perkin Elmer NexION 350D / PE 350D)
IWA-35EP laser liquid water isotope analyser with LGR standards
Hot spring water chemistry and isotope data from a 16S rRNA microbial census (Hou et al. 2013)
Redox control of U mobility: U(VI) mobile, U(IV) immobile
Adsorption of uranium on clay minerals (Ames et al. 1983; Bao et al. 2021; Davey & Scott 1956)
Typical U contents of sandstone, shale, limestone and granite (Kathren 1984)

novelty_claims.quote: For the hot spring deposits at Tengchong, however, they are not yet studied in the aspect of elemental geochemistry.
For the continental rift-related geothermal system, the hydrothermal alteration zones are rarely studied for uranium exploration.

limits: Single-author study. The sample sets are small: five waters and five deposit analyses (two are from the same GPS 185 locality). The headline altered-sandstone U values (14–36 ppm) come from Xiao et al. (2017), not from new measurements, and the water REE and Eh values are also taken from the literature. No uranium minerals are identified in the new samples, and no U speciation, U-series dating or mass balance is done. The U mechanism (granite leaching, fault transport, decompression, fixation) is adopted from Li (1992) and Li et al. (1997) without stated rivals or a discriminating test, so 'best_explanation' is applied loosely; inference: no alternative such as a detrital or sedimentary U source in the Nanlin sandstones is discussed. Composition is none_fits because conditions are found and several reservoirs are compared, but no rivals are stated for the main claim and the observations do not stand in for varied auxiliaries, so neither trace_series nor natures_repetition fits. There are internal inconsistencies: Figure 8 gives sinter U as 1–2 ppm, while the text gives 0.3–1.9 ppm for most deposits; the introduction cites earlier water U of 2.6–36 ppb, while new waters are 0–2.7 ppb, and this difference is not discussed. A peer review history is said to exist at Publons, but it was not supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the acknowledgement says that reviewer comments improved the manuscript. No disagreement with published work is explicitly stated: comparisons with Nevada and Tibet sinters and with tufas are presented as contrasts in magnitude, not challenges. Sub-claims: meteoric origin of the water (kept from isotope comparison); deposits precipitated under reduced conditions (best_explanation); HREE enrichment of the sandstones from clay mobilization (best_explanation, cited mechanism); sulfates and clay zones as prospecting indicators (a recommendation, not tested).

alternatives_considered.alternatives: enhanced water-rock interaction; evaporation due to varying temperatures
water-rock interactions; magma degassing (as origin of dissolved solutes)
